questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had been to Mexico before and wanted to return in an academic setting and to experience living there for a longer period. I chose UNAM because Mexico City is a beautiful, bustling and exciting city and I had heard only great things about UNAM in general and the Facultad de Filosofía y Letras in particular.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Once I was physically on campus and met everybody in person, everything was quite straightforward. The programme during the introduction days really covered everything important, but had I had additional questions, I could have sent a mail, where I in general received swift replies, or gone straight to the offices.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were held two introduction days roughly a week in advance of the official semester start (attendance was mandatory). During these days, we received all relevant practical information, went through different workshops on living abroad and mental health, got a tour of campus and our faculty building, etc. This was also where I got to meet all the other exchange students and the professors that I had been chatting with over mail during my preparations for the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found accommodation in advance through a website called "roomgo". This was no doubt a risky thing to do and I'd always recommend arriving a few weeks in advance and find housing once you are there and able to physically see the place and talk to the casero in person. There are websites and several Facebook groups, but you could even just walk through the area of interest and ask people/write to the WhatsApp numbers on the housing announcements you see, to find something. My impression was that it is easy to find good housing with the budget of a danish student on SU.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I stayed in Coyoacán and went to uni by bike. It's a beautiful and safe area that I can only recommend. If you would like to be closer to campus (maybe even walking distance), Copilco is a good option. If you want to stay more towards the city centre or if you rely on public transport, I would prioritise living close to the metro line 3 (Indios verdes - universidad) or the metrobus line 1 which runs along Insurgentes. Check where your faculty is located on campus because Ciudad Universitaria is huge, so something being close to campus does not equal that it's close to where you will be going.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Courses where selected a few weeks in advance of the semester start, and after the first week of classes, you had the opportunity to switch courses, so you only committed to the courses after having met the professor and gotten a good impression of the course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was always the option to contact the people responsible for exchange students in person or through mail, and in the first week of courses, you had the opportunity to talk to the professors and get all the doubts out of the way.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I enrolled in all the courses that I had selected, but I ended up taking very different courses than I thought when planning the exchange because the final course catalogue was only published so last minute.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress too much about any course selections that you have to give at any point prior to the actual enrolment, everything will change when you receive the final course catalogue anyways. Personally, I had to apply for forhåndsgodkendelse several times because the deadlines from KU didn't match the reality at UNAM.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took courses that were for students on the 6th or 4th semester. Overall, I found them adequately challenging, but had I been completely fluent in Spanish when I arrived or had I actually been a philosophy student, they would have probably been on the easy side.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the small group sizes, which varied from 4-20 people. All my courses were taught seminar-style as opposed to classical lectures, which made learning interesting and much more discussion- and dialogue-based. It also made for a relaxed learning environment and very approachable professors. Finally, I learned a ton writing my final exam essays, both because of working on relatively large and open projects independently and through writing so many pages in Spanish. All in all, everything seemed much more personal, flexible and not so set-in-stone.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Filosofía en México with Alejandro Sánchez González 
Problemas de Filosofía del Lenguaje with Esteban Withrington (on philosophy of mind)
Problemas de Teoría del Conocimiento y Filosofía de la Ciencia with Xenia Rueda
Problemas de Teoría del Conocimiento y Filosofía de la Ciencia with Claudia Lorena García (on cognitive science) 
Seminario optativo with Ernesto Priani (on AI)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend taking any Filosofía en México course (mine with Alejandro was really interesting and the exam was easy). That is really a must, no matter what you are studying. The seminar with Ernesto Priani was also a true gem. I learned a ton there and the teaching methods were out of this world and something you rarely see at universities. The philosophy of mind course with Esteban Withrington was a great and thorough introduction to all the classics in the field, and the professor gave a lot of interesting expansions on different topics, and was also great of showing the connections between the different texts and ideas.

questions.answer: There was a small insurance that UNAM had us sign and pay for (maybe 100kr).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything was roughly what I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything you could possibly imagine. A ton of free sports clubs as well as free gyms and a free open air swimming stadium, museums, cinema, and discounts/free entry on more museums and cinemas and other activities around the city and even around the country.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go to Cineteca Nacional in Coyoacán (students pay 20kr, the architecture is stunning and all films they show are great). I took salsa classes in Coyoacán with La Gozadera (Salsaficción on Google Maps) which were SO much fun, a beautiful group of people.
On campus, I recommend going through the hassle of making the health check at the medical centre to be able to enter the alberca olímpica area for yoga classes, swimming, gym, etc. It's worth it.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Become friends with a Mexican exchange student so they can take you to their pueblo. Whenever somebody invites you into their home, say yes. 
Apart from that, Tepotzlan and Cuernavaca make for nice day trips. Grutas de Tolantongo is, in my opinion, a must, and even though it is a hassle to get there on your own by public transport, I recommend you do it and stay the night. Do NOT go there on public holidays, but try doing it during the week. Guanajuato (the city) has a very special vibe to it and is definitely worth a visit. For larger holidays, the state of Oaxaca is truly magical.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy, but it wasn't my first time either. People are so kind, welcoming and open, especially when you speak Spanish and show some curiosity. Even more if you eat the spicy food.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is totally socially acceptable to just walk up to someone and ask if you can sit and strike up a conversation. Personally, I feel like I had made friends during the introduction days before I had even thought about it or made an effort. If you don't get that lucky during the first days, there are several events for exchange students during the semester, both through UNAM and external organisations, so there a plenty of opportunities to make a friend.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Managing the difference between KU's deadlines and bureaucratic requirements and the drastically different reality in Mexico.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The people, the food, the dancing, the laughing, the Mexican side of social media, comidas where people of all generations are invited, and of course the language.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Don't stress about all the deadlines and requirements from KU. Just work your way through it one thing at a time and trust the process. It will all work out and if something goes wrong, Mexican culture is on your side because it is all about improvising and problem-solving along the way. 
Don't speak English, even if it's hard in Spanish, even if you feel stupid. To list all the reasons for this would exceed this format.
Select your courses so that your timetable gives you a long weekend (e.g. a Monday or Friday of). That way, every weekend is a long weekend and you can go on more small trips and explore the rest of the country.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: UNAM is a huge deal. Be grateful if you get to go. It is a really respected institution with heaps of history and significance in the Spanish speaking world, and that is an energy you can really feel once you a there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Eating lunch with my friends every day at the cafeteria on campus, gossiping and laughing together before returning to the library in the afternoon to study in silent company. And every time a classmate gave me a recommendation for a book or a paper that might fit into my interests.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The sheer size of the city. It took an hour to get anywhere, which was a big contrast to hopping on your bike and being there in 10 minutes in Copenhagen. And the air quality was baaaad and dries your whole body out. I even got nosebleeds. So be prepared and bring a lot of moisturiser...

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
